newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief backs multinational force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief backs multinational force for Zaire.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali threw his support on Friday behind the dispatch of a multinational military force to deal with a looming catastrophe in eastern Zaire, where more than a million refugees are without food and medical care.
The Security Council is already considering a resolution to set up such a force.
"Given the need for urgent action if tens of thousands of lives are to be saved, time is of the essence," Boutros-Ghali said in a letter to Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia.
He said it would take too long to deploy a U.N. peace-keeping force or one set up by countries of the region.

The best option would be if U.N. members "with the necessary capacity would take the lead in putting together a multinational force, in consultation with the secretary-general of the OAU (Organization of African Unity) and the regional states concerned, and would seek the Security Council's authorisation to deploy it."
Boutros-Ghali, whose letter was dated Thursday, said he therefore welcomed the fact the council was "focusing its attention on this option."

He was alluding to a resolution circulated by France that would authorise the establishment of a multinational force for a two-month period to allow the safe delivery of humanitarian aid to refugees and others at risk in eastern Zaire.
The draft was being discussed by council members during closed-door consultations on Friday but there was no immediate indication when it might be adopted.

"The international community now faces a situation in which a million or more people are scattered in eastern Zaire beyond the reach of the agencies which can provide them with food and medical care," Boutros-Ghali said.
"Unless effective action is taken urgently, many tens of thousands of human beings are going to die of hunger and disease."

The proposed force would secure airfields and border crossing points and protect logistic supply bases in eastern Zaire. It would also identify and protect accessible locations where scattered refugees could be concentrated to receive aid.

But Boutros-Ghali said the crisis was not only a humanitarian one since recent events had proved peace and security would not be restored to the Great Lakes region of Africa unless the refugee problems created by the internal conflicts in Burundi and Rwanda were resolved.

He was referring to hundreds of thousands of people who fled fighting between Hutus and minority Tutsis in both countries. They include members of the former Rwandan Hutu-led army and militias responsible for the genocidal massacre of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.

These former fighters, hoping eventually to regain power but fearing retribution from Rwanda's current Tutsi-led government if they return now, have prevented other Hutu refugees from being repatriated.

"It will therefore be necessary to ensure that the short-term response does not re-create conditions in which refugees can again be intimidated by those who, for political reasons, do not want them to return to their home countries," Boutros-Ghali said.
"On the contrary, the international community's response to this humanitarian crisis must mark the beginning of a new programme of repatriation."
